title: Language Modeling Fundamentals
summary: What a language model actually predicts, from n-grams to neural LMs, and how it's evaluated.

slides.subTitle: Next-token probability — and why it's so powerful
slides.markdown: A language model does exactly one thing: given a sequence of tokens, it outputs a probability distribution over what token comes next. That's it — no built-in notion of "facts", "reasoning", or "conversation". What makes this primitive so powerful is that **predicting the next word well requires implicitly learning grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and style**, because all of those show up in what word is likely to come next. "The capital of France is ___" forces the model to have learned a fact to predict "Paris" with high probability; "If it's raining, you should bring an ___" forces basic causal reasoning to predict "umbrella". Modern LLMs are, mechanically, still just this — next-token prediction — scaled up enormously.

slides.subTitle: The sparsity problem that limits them
slides.markdown: The earliest language models estimated next-word probability purely by counting: P(word | previous n-1 words) = count of that n-gram in a training corpus, divided by the count of the preceding (n-1)-gram. This works for common phrases but breaks down fast: most possible n-grams (especially for n ≥ 3) **never appear** in even a huge training corpus, so their counted probability is zero — a phenomenon called **sparsity**. Smoothing techniques (Laplace smoothing, backoff to shorter n-grams) patch this but don't fix the underlying issue: counting can't generalize to a novel-but-plausible phrase it never saw. This is exactly the gap neural language models close, by learning a continuous representation that generalizes across similar contexts instead of counting exact matches.

slides.subTitle: RNN-based, then Transformer-based
slides.markdown: Neural LMs replace counting with a learned function: an RNN (or later, a Transformer decoder) reads the preceding tokens and outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next one, trained by maximizing the likelihood of the actual next token across a huge corpus. RNN-based LMs improved on n-grams by generalizing across similar contexts via learned embeddings, but still struggled with long-range dependencies due to vanishing gradients over many time steps. Transformer-based LMs (GPT and its successors) removed that limitation via self-attention, letting every position directly reference any earlier token regardless of distance — this is the architecture behind every modern large language model, covered in depth under [Attention & Transformer Architecture](attention-transformer-architecture).

slides.subTitle: How language models are evaluated
slides.markdown: **Perplexity** measures how "surprised" a language model is by held-out test text — mathematically, it's the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood the model assigns to the true next tokens. Lower perplexity means the model consistently assigned higher probability to what actually came next, i.e. it's a better fit to the language distribution. Intuitively, a perplexity of 20 means the model is, on average, as uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly among 20 equally likely next tokens at each step. Perplexity is cheap to compute (no human judgment needed) and correlates reasonably well with downstream quality, which is why it remains the standard intrinsic metric for comparing LMs during pretraining.

slides.subTitle: Different tokenizers, different vocabularies
slides.markdown: A common mistake: comparing perplexity numbers across two models trained with **different tokenizers or vocabulary sizes** and concluding one is "better". Perplexity is computed per token, and what counts as "one token" differs across tokenizers — a model with a larger vocabulary (more whole words, fewer subword splits) tends to report lower perplexity per token simply because each token carries more information, not necessarily because the model understands language better. Valid perplexity comparisons require the **same tokenizer and vocabulary** on both sides, or normalizing to a token-independent unit like bits-per-character. Skipping this check is a classic way to draw a wrong conclusion from a right-looking number.

slides.sectionTitle: From language modeling to few-shot generalization
slides.subTitle: Why scale changed everything
slides.markdown: For decades, language modeling was viewed as a narrow benchmark task — predict the next word, measure perplexity, done. What changed: at sufficient model and data scale, next-token prediction alone produces models that can perform tasks they were **never explicitly trained on** — translation, summarization, arithmetic, code — just from a few examples in the prompt (**few-shot learning**), or sometimes zero examples at all. This emergent generalization is why the field's center of gravity shifted from task-specific fine-tuned models to a single, massive, pretrained language model prompted for many tasks — the subject of [LLM Architecture & Scaling](llm-architecture-scaling).

slides.subTitle: Laplace smoothing rescues a zero-count bigram
slides.markdown:
Say your training corpus has 1,000 occurrences of "thank", 400 of which are followed by "you" — so raw counting gives P(you | thank) = 400/1000 = 0.4. But the bigram "thank goodness" never happened to appear, so raw counting gives it probability exactly **0** — meaning any test sentence containing it gets assigned zero probability overall, which is clearly wrong (it's a perfectly normal phrase, just unlucky not to appear in training).

**Laplace (add-one) smoothing** adds 1 to every count before dividing, across a vocabulary of size V: P(goodness | thank) becomes `(0+1) / (1000+V)` instead of `0/1000` — small, but no longer zero. This is a blunt fix (it steals a little probability mass from every seen bigram to cover unseen ones) but it's exactly why n-gram models needed **smoothing** as a mandatory add-on, not an optional refinement — without it, encountering any single unseen n-gram would zero out an entire sentence's probability.

slides.subTitle: Exposure bias in autoregressive generation
slides.markdown:
During training, an autoregressive LM predicts each next token conditioned on the **true, gold** preceding tokens (a technique called teacher forcing) — it never has to condition on its own possibly-wrong past output. At generation time, though, every token it conditions on **is** its own prior output, errors included.

This mismatch is called **exposure bias**: a small mistake early in generation shifts the model into a context distribution it never trained on, and errors can compound rather than self-correct — the model has no experience recovering from its own wrong turn, because training never showed it one. It's part of why generation quality can degrade over long outputs even when the model's next-token accuracy looks excellent on held-out gold-context evaluation.

slides.subTitle: Lower perplexity doesn't guarantee better downstream performance
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Model A has lower perplexity than Model B on our held-out set, so Model A will be the better model for our actual product."

**Why it's wrong:** perplexity measures fit to the **next-token distribution of the evaluation text**, which is a proxy for the actual downstream task, not the task itself — it says nothing about instruction-following, factual accuracy, safety, or how well the model performs on the specific task your product needs. A model can have modestly higher perplexity yet be dramatically better at the actual product task (e.g. it was fine-tuned or aligned in a way that trades a bit of raw next-token fit for behavior humans prefer).

**Correct model:** use perplexity as a cheap, useful signal **during pretraining** to catch regressions or compare checkpoints of the same model family (holding tokenizer constant, per the earlier pitfall), but validate any real decision with task-specific evaluation, not perplexity alone.
